title: Does the Race of the Stranger Matter? Investigating Toddlers’ Wariness Towards Familiar and Unfamiliar Race Strangers
content: Within the first year of life, infants can perceptually discriminate people by race. However, beyond perceptual discrimination, it remains unclear whether infants use race to guide their social behaviors, such as whether they approach or withdraw from people of different races. This question is particularly understudied during toddlerhood (between 1 and 2 years of age), before children can reliably report racial attitudes around 3 to 4 years of age. The present study examined whether 12- to 25-month-old U.S. toddlers (N = 118) show greater wariness toward strangers from unfamiliar than familiar racial groups in a within-subject design to determine whether toddlers use a person’s race to guide their social behaviors. Toddlers did not exhibit significantly greater wariness toward strangers from unfamiliar than familiar racial groups, and this pattern was not moderated by their racial backgrounds, temperament, or racial diversity of their social networks or neighborhoods. These findings suggest that race may not function as a salient cue for guiding toddlers’ social responses during the second year of life. More broadly, these findings contribute to growing evidence that early perceptual sensitivity to race does not necessarily entail race-based biases in evaluations or behaviors in early childhood.
